docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: This course provides an overview of robot mechanisms, dynamics, and intelligent controls. Topics include planar and spatial kinematics, and motion planning; mechanism design for manipulators and mobile robots, multi-rigid-body dynamics, 3D graphic simulation; control design, actuators, and sensors; wireless networking, task modeling, human-machine interface, and embedded software.

docs.title: Course Info
docs.text:
Instructor: Oliver Ochoa Garcia

Contact: oliver.ochoa2@iberopuebla.mx

Department: Department of Science and Engineering

Credits: 8

Obligatory Pre-requisites: 12188 "Analysis of dynamic systems"

Recommended Pre-requisites: 12198 "Discrete control", 12202 "Embedded systems", 12262 "Advanced Static and Dynamics"

docs.title: Course Meeting Times
docs.text: Lectures: 2 sessions / week, 2 hours / session - Tuesday, 15:00 - 17:00 - Thursday, 15:00 - 17:00

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Math: single & multivariable calculus; linear algebra (vectors, matrix ops, rank/nullspace, Jacobian, SVD/conditioning); basic ODEs (1st/2nd order).
  • Mechanics: rigid-body kinematics; statics/dynamics (Newton–Euler or work–energy) at an undergraduate level.
  • Control basics: LTI step response specs (rise/settling/overshoot), PD/PID fundamentals, discrete-time sampling, saturation & anti-windup conceptually.
  • Programming: Python (NumPy, basic plotting), Git fundamentals (clone/commit/branch/merge), Linux shell (WSL2 terminal navigation, packages).
  • Electronics: DC motors/encoders/servos, PWM & H-bridge, basic ADC, safe power (current limits, fusing, LiPo handling).
  • Tools readiness: Laptop that runs WSL2 + Ubuntu 24.04, VS Code, Python 3.10+, 30–50 GB free disk; internet access in lab.

docs.title: Robot Definition
docs.text:
“A goal oriented machine that can sense, plan, and act.” — Peter Corke

A robot perceives its surroundings and, guided by a goal, decides on an action to take. That action could be moving the end-effector of a robotic arm to pick up an object, or navigating a mobile robot to a specific location, in other words that physically interacts with the environment.

Is it a robot?

Industrial robot arm (car assembly line)

Robot

An industrial manipulator that:

  • Senses: joint encoders, sometimes force/torque sensors or safety scanners
  • Plans: trajectories to weld, paint, or assemble according to a production goal
  • Acts: moves its joints and end-effector to manipulate parts
Simple electric drill

Not a robot

  • Acts: spins when the trigger is pressed
  • Missing: no autonomous sensing of the environment, no planning toward a goal
  • It simply executes the user’s direct command.
Desktop or laptop computer

Not a robot (by itself)

  • Can run planning algorithms, but:
  • Does not typically sense the physical environment in a robotics sense.
  • Does not act on the physical world (no wheels, no motors, no grippers).
  • Better thought of as a possible “brain” for a robot, not the robot itself.
Autonomous vacuum cleaner

Robot

A mobile platform that:

  • Senses: bump sensors, cliff sensors, sometimes cameras or LiDAR
  • Plans: coverage paths, obstacle avoidance, and how to return to the dock
  • Acts: drives its wheels and controls suction to achieve the goal of cleaning
Washing machine

Not a robot

  • Runs a preprogrammed script (wash → rinse → spin).
  • Limited sensing (e.g., water level), but it does not choose actions based on a high-level goal.
  • Considered an automated machine, not a sense–plan–act robot.
Remote-controlled toy car

Not a robot

  • The human does all the sensing and planning.
  • The car just follows direct commands (forward, turn, stop).
  • No autonomous goal-directed behavior.
Smart speaker / voice assistant

Not a robot

  • Senses: audio via microphones.
  • Plans: decides on responses or cloud actions.
  • Acts: mainly outputs sound or data; no movement or manipulation.
  • An intelligent interface, not a physical robot.
3D printer or CNC machine

Not a robot

  • Acts: moves a toolhead very precisely.
  • Senses: minimal (limit switches, basic feedback).
  • Executes a fixed program (G-code) rather than planning actions to achieve a high-level goal.
  • Depending on the definition used (industrial robotics vs autonomy-focused), CNC/3D printers may be classified as robots; here we treat them as automated machines because they typically do not plan actions toward a high-level goal.
Quadcopter drone

Robot

A flying platform that:

  • Senses: IMU (accelerometers, gyroscopes), GPS, barometer, sometimes cameras or LiDAR
  • Plans: stabilizes its attitude, follows waypoints, avoids obstacles, or tracks targets
  • Acts: controls its motors and propellers to move and hover in 3D space toward a goal (e.g., hold position, follow a path, film a subject)

docs.title: Types of robots
docs.text:
Robots can be classified in many different ways. Here are some common taxonomies:

  • By application domain: industrial robots, service robots, medical robots, agricultural robots, military robots, space robots, etc.

  • By morphology: manipulators (robot arms), mobile robots (wheeled, legged, aerial, underwater), humanoid robots, swarm robots, etc.

  • By autonomy level: teleoperated robots, semi-autonomous robots, fully autonomous robots.

Robots by morphology

Manipulators

Designed to work in a fixed workspace, these robots stand out for their ability to perform precise, repetitive tasks. Manipulator robots are defined by the joint structure that connects the base to the end-effector. They are often used in industrial settings for tasks such as assembly, welding, and painting. We can find them as RRR, RRP, or other combinations of revolute (R) and prismatic (P) joints.

The main examples are:

  • Cartesian Robots (PPP)
  • SCARA Robots (RRP)
  • Articulated Robots (RRR)
  • Spherical Robots (RRP)
  • Cylindrical Robots (RPP)
  • Delta Robots (Parallel)

Mobile Robots

Designed to move through their environment, either autonomously or under control, across different spaces. They are defined by their locomotion method. Typically used for exploration, transportation, and service tasks.

The main examples are:

  • Wheeled robots
  • Legged robots
  • Tracked robots
  • Aerial robots (drones / UAVs)
  • Underwater robots (ROVs / AUVs)

Hybrid Robots

Hybrid robots combine mobility and manipulation capabilities in a single system, or integrate multiple types of robotic structures to perform complex tasks. A typical example is a mobile platform equipped with one or more robotic arms, or a humanoid robot that can both walk and grasp objects. These robots are usually designed for highly specific or demanding tasks that require moving through the environment and physically interacting with it.

docs.title: Degrees of Freedom
docs.text:
configuration: a specification of the positions of all the points of a mechanism

degrees of freedom (dof): number of real numbers required to describe a configuration

In a rigid body, the dof corresponds to the number of independent displacements (translations and rotations) that the body can undergo in space.

  • dof of a planar body: m = 3

  • dof of a spatial body: m = 6

To represent a robot we assume it is made up of rigid bodies (links) connected by joints. The total dof of the robot is determined by the number of links and the types of joints connecting them.

docs.title: Joint Types
docs.text:
There are several basic types of robot joints.

A 0-DOF joint is called the Fixed Joint , where the child link is rigidly connected to the parent link.

1-DOF Joints:

  • The revolute joint (R), also called a hinge joint, allows rotational motion about the joint axis
    • Rotational motion with no limit is called a Continuous Joint
  • The prismatic joint (P), also called a sliding or linear joint, allows translational (or rectilinear) motion along the direction of the joint axis
  • The helical joint (H), also called a screw joint, allows simultaneous rotation and translation about a screw axis.

Multiple DOF Joints:

  • The cylindrical joint (C) has two DOF and allows independent translations and rotations about a single fixed joint axis
  • The universal joint (U) is another two-DOF joint that consists of a pair of revolute joints arranged so that their joint axes are orthogonal
  • The spherical joint (S), also called a ball-and-socket joint, has three DOF and functions much like our shoulder joint.
  • The planar joint allows two translational and one rotational motion in a plane.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
\(\mathbb{R}^n\) in this context represents possible states or positions in translation.

\(S^1\) in this context represents possible states or positions in rotation.

We describe the position of a robot's links and joints using the configuration space.

docs.title: Configuration Space (C-space)
docs.text:
Definition. The configuration of a robot is a complete specification of the position of every point of the robot. The minimum number n needed to represent the configuration is the number of degrees of freedom (dof) of the robot. The n-dimensional space containing all possible configurations of the robot is called the configuration space (C-space). The configuration of a robot is represented by a point in its C-space.

  • Examples (Different topologies with a two-dimensional C-space):

docs.title: Workspace (W-space)
docs.text:
Definition. The set of end-effector poses (position/orientation) attainable by some configuration(s) \(q\). Often we study just positions (e.g., tip position in the plane) or full poses in 3D space \(SE(3)\).

Sometimes we can classify them as:

  • Reachable workspace: poses attainable in at least one orientation.
  • Dexterous workspace: poses where all orientations (or a specified set) are attainable; a subset of reachable.

Different \(q\) can map to the same point in W-space. Therefore, there exists a mapping \(x = f(q)\) from C-space to W-space, where \(x\) is the end-effector pose in W-space.

For example, 2R planar arm: - C-space: \(S^1 \times S^1\) (torus) - W-space: an annulus with radii - min radius = \(|l_1 - l_2|\) - max radius = \(l_1 + l_2\)

Which would mean The workspace is the image of \(C\) under \(f\); many \(q\) can map to the same \(x\).

Nomenclature

  • \(q \in C\): configuration (joint variables).
  • \(x \in W\): task/pose (position/orientation).

Here are some demonstrations on a simulator.

docs.title: Constraints in Robotics — Holonomic, Non-holonomic, and Pfaffian Form
1) Where constraints live
docs.text:
• Configuration space \( \mathcal{C} \): points \( q \) (configurations).
  • Tangent space \( T_q\mathcal{C} \): vectors \( \dot q \) (instantaneous motions at \( q \)).
  • Workspace \( \mathcal{W} \): points \( x \) (end-effector poses); velocities \( \dot x \in T_x\mathcal{W} \).

Key idea. Holonomic constraints carve subsets of \( \mathcal{C} \) (where you may be). Non-holonomic constraints restrict directions in \( T_q\mathcal{C} \) (how you may move instantaneously).

docs.title: 2) Holonomic constraints (position-level)
docs.text:
Definition. Integrable relations on configuration: $$ g(q) = 0, \qquad h(q) \le 0 . $$

Where: - \( q \in \mathcal{C} \): configuration (joint angles/lengths, etc.). - \( g:\mathcal{C}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{k} \): equality constraints (e.g., loop closure). - \( h:\mathcal{C}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{m} \): inequality constraints (e.g., joint limits, collision buffers).

  • Effect: Remove configurations from \( \mathcal{C} \).
  • Examples:
  • Joint limits: \( \theta_i^{\min} \le \theta_i \le \theta_i^{\max} \).
  • Loop-closure equations in closed chains.
  • Collision/obstacle avoidance inequalities.
  • Planning view: Treat as forbidden sets in \( \mathcal{C} \). They can change the topology (disconnect components, create holes).

docs.title: 3) Non-holonomic constraints (velocity-level)
docs.text:
Definition. Linear constraints on velocities, typically Pfaffian: $$ A(q)\,\dot q = 0 . $$

Where: - \( A(q) \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times n} \): rows are linear one-forms (each row = one instantaneous restriction). - \( \dot q \in T_q\mathcal{C} \): generalized velocity.

  • Effect: Restrict instantaneous directions in \( T_q\mathcal{C} \); do not directly remove configurations.
  • Non-integrability: There is no globally valid \( g(q)=0 \) equivalent on the same domain.
  • Intuition: Though some instantaneous motions are forbidden (e.g., sideways slide), you can often reach many configurations by sequencing admissible motions (e.g., parallel parking).

docs.title: 4) Holonomic vs Non-holonomic — quick contrasts
docs.text: Aspect Holonomic Non-holonomic Mathematical form \( g(q)=0,\ h(q)\le0 \) \( A(q)\dot q=0 \) (Pfaffian) Lives in \( \mathcal{C} \) (configuration set) \( T_q\mathcal{C} \) (velocity directions) Primary effect Removes configurations Removes instantaneous directions Integrability By definition integrable Not integrable to equivalent \( g(q)=0 \) Canonical example Joint limits, loop closure No-slip wheel, knife-edge skid Planning impact C-obstacles/feasible sets Paths built from admissible motions

docs.title: 5) Nomenclature (spaces)
docs.text:
• \( q \in \mathcal{C} \): configuration (joint variables).
  • \( \dot q \in T_q\mathcal{C} \): instantaneous motion.
  • \( x \in \mathcal{W} \), \( \dot x \in T_x\mathcal{W} \): pose and velocity in workspace.
  • Holonomic: \( g(q)=0 \), \( h(q)\le0 \).
  • Non-holonomic (Pfaffian): \( A(q)\dot q=0 \).
  • Inputs: \( \dot q = B(q)u \) with \( A(q)B(q)u=0 \).

Quick mnemonic: Holonomic = where; Non-holonomic = how.

docs.title: 1. Install WSL2 and Ubuntu 24.04
docs.text:
• If you are already on native Ubuntu: skip this Step 1 entirely (WSL2 + Ubuntu installation).
  • If you are on Windows 11: follow all steps.

WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux 2) is an improved version of WSL that allows you to run native Linux distributions on Windows without traditional virtual machines.

Open PowerShell as administrator:

wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

This command:

  • Enables Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) and the Virtual Machine Platform
  • Sets WSL2 as the default version
  • Downloads and installs Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble Numbat is the current stable distro)

docs.title: 2. First boot and system update
docs.text:
If you are on Windows, launch Ubuntu (from the Start menu) and create a UNIX username/password (the password will not show characters while you type). Then run:

sudo apt update
sudo apt full-upgrade -y

This will update Ubuntu.

docs.title: 3. System configuration for ROS 2
docs.text: Before installing ROS, we need to configure the system for compatibility.

docs.title: 3.1 Configure locale (text encoding)
docs.text:
First, configure the locale (system language/encoding settings). ROS uses UTF-8, which prevents issues with special characters in ROS and other programs.

sudo apt update && sudo apt install locales
sudo locale-gen en_US en_US.UTF-8
sudo update-locale LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 LANG=en_US.UTF-8
export LANG=en_US.UTF-8

These settings use US English, but any UTF-8 locale works.

locale # Verify it is UTF-8

docs.title: 3.2 Enable “universe” and add the ROS 2 repository
docs.text:
First, make sure the Ubuntu Universe repository is enabled.

sudo apt install -y software-properties-common
sudo add-apt-repository universe

Now add the ROS 2 GPG key (for apt):

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y curl
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ros/rosdistro/master/ros.key \
  | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/ros-archive-keyring.gpg

Finally, add the repository to your sources list:

echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/ros-archive-keyring.gpg] \
  http://packages.ros.org/ros2/ubuntu \
  $(. /etc/os-release && echo $UBUNTU_CODENAME) main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ros2.list > /dev/null

docs.title: 4. Install ROS 2 Jazzy Desktop
docs.text:
Update apt to include the changes:

sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade

Install the full desktop distribution:

sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop

docs.title: 5. Verify the installation with an example
docs.text:
First, configure the environment. Add ROS setup to your startup file (~/.bashrc) so ROS commands are available every time you open a terminal:

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash

For this test you will need two terminals, so open a second terminal.

In one terminal run a simple C++ node called talker:

ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker

In the other terminal run a Python node called listener:

ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener

You should see the talker printing Publishing: numbers and the listener printing I heard: numbers, matching the messages. This verifies both the C++ and Python APIs.

We can verify our packages installation with:

ros2 pkg list

We can also list all executables with:

ros2 pkg executables

And filter executables per package with:

ros2 pkg executables <pkg_name>

For example, with turtlesim:

ros2 pkg executables turtlesim

To see usage options for ros2 run:

ros2 run -h

To run an executable:

ros2 run <package_name> <executable_name> # RUN structure
ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node         # EXAMPLE RUN

This will run the following sim:

To test communication, run a new executable from the turtlesim package that lets you move the turtle with the keyboard:

ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key

How does this work? ROS 2 acts as middleware, in other words a communication network between different processes, encompassing all executables and connections between them.

!!! You can look at more info here: https://docs.ros.org/en/kilted/Tutorials/Beginner-CLI-Tools/Understanding-ROS2-Nodes/Understanding-ROS2-Nodes.html

gz sim shapes.sdf

docs.text:
To work with ROS in VS Code, we will install the ROS extension. Robotcis Developer Environment. WHich you cna find in the Extensions tab (Ctrl+Shift+X) by searching for "ROS". As we have a windows system with WSL2, make sure to install the extension in WSL. Byr running:

code .

docs.title: Sourcing ROS 2
docs.text:
setup.bash is a shell script that prepares your current terminal to use ROS (and/or your ROS workspace).

it typically:

  • Defines core environment variables so ROS can find packages and resources
  • Extends your PATH so commands become available
  • Updates library paths so binaries can find shared libraries at runtime

source is a shell built-in command (bash/zsh) that runs a script in your current terminal session.

We need to do this every time we open a new terminal, or add it to our shell startup file (e.g., ~/.bashrc for bash) to do it automatically.

To add it to your ~/.bashrc, you can:

open vscode on the home folder, open .bashrc and add at the end:

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash

Then, either restart your terminal or run:

source ~/.bashrc

docs.title: ROS 2 Concepts
docs.text:
ROS 2 consists of packages and manifests:

  • packages are the basic organizational unit. They consist of a collection of related files and directories used to organize and manage ROS 2 nodes, libraries, and resources.
  • manifests describe the packages, normally in a file named package.xml, which contains metadata.

docs.title: ROS basic terms:
docs.text: Term Description Underlying communication layer (DDS) Provides high-performance, reliable, real-time data communication and integration capabilities, enabling messaging and service invocation between nodes in ROS 2. Node The smallest unit of processing in ROS. It is typically an executable. Each node can use topics or services to communicate with other nodes. Message A data structure composed of fields of types such as int, float, and boolean. Topic A one-way, asynchronous communication mechanism. By publishing to or subscribing from topics, nodes can exchange data. The topic type is determined by the message type. Publishing Sending data using a message type corresponding to the topic content. Publishers Nodes that publish messages on topics. Subscribing Receiving data using the message type corresponding to the topic content. Subscribers Nodes that receive messages from publishers on topics they subscribe to. Services A bidirectional, synchronous communication mechanism where a client requests a task and a server responds. Service Servers A node that takes requests as input and provides responses as output. Service Clients A node that sends requests and receives responses.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
It's a bundle of files in a folder which can be reused, kind of like an application or library.

Inside a package, you can have:

  • code(Nodes, Topics, Services, etc.)
  • needs (dependencies, types, etc.)
  • build instructions (CMakeLists.txt, package.xml)
  • Extras Like:
    • launch files
    • parameter files
    • custom message types

It's build using ament and colcon through Cmake if written in C++ or setup.py if written in Python. For this class, we will be using Python.

In python language the minimum files in a package are: - package.xml Meta information, like name, version, programmer, dependencies, etc. - setup.py installer reipe for colcon, what to include, scripts, etc. - resource/<package_name> Marker that helps python tools to find the package. - setup.cfg Shows where your runnable files are located. - <package_name>/__init__.py the real package folder which will be used to build.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
A node is the smallest unit of processing in ROS. It is typically an executable. Each node can use topics or services to communicate with other nodes.

It's main characteristics are: - Small program/process - They shoul be for a single purpose - They can either send or receive information - They're written in different languages (C++, Python, etc.) and still work together

They're basically executables therefore the syntax to run them is:

ros2 run <package_name> <executable_name>

# Example
ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node

Each robot is composed of multiple nodes, which we will need to monitor and manage. We can list all the nodes running in our system using:

ros2 node list

each node will need its own executable running, so at the beginning we will have to open multiple terminals to launch each node.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
Topics are a one-way, asynchronous communication mechanism. By publishing to or subscribing from topics, nodes can exchange data. The topic type is determined by the message type.

  • They are the buses between nodes
  • They are one-way
  • They are asynchronous
  • They can be one to many, many to one, many to many
  • They dont need to know the node theyre communicating with
  • They need to be a specific type of data(i.e. )

To interact with topics nodes can have on of two roles, either as publishers or subscribers.

  • Publishers send data to topics
  • Subscribers receive data from topics

we can check all the active topics with the command: 

ros2 topic list
and then we can check the type of each topic by adding the -t flag, to the endof the command.

We can also check the data being transmitted in a topic using: 

ros2 topic echo <topic_name>
As explained before topics can be many to many, one to many, many to one, etc. To check how many publishers and subscribers are connected to a topic we can use: 
ros2 topic info <topic_name> --verbose

Topics can also have types, which is how they are encoded and everyone must agree with the format to be able to communicate. We can either use built-in types or create custom ones. Common built-in types are: - std_msgs(strings, integers, booleans, etc.) - geometry_msgs(poses, transforms, velocities, etc.) - sensor_msgs(images, IMU, laser scans, etc.) - nav_msgs(odometry, maps, etc.)

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Services are another way to communicate between nodes, however instead of being continuous it's a one and done communication.

  • They are bidirectional
  • They are synchronous
  • Not for continuous data streams
  • They need a client and server

you can check the available services using: 

ros2 service list

Services also have types, except that they are in two parts, a request and a response. We can check the type of a service using: 

ros2 service type <service_name>
similarly to topics you can use list, -t, info --verbose, and echo commands to get more information about services. As well as find to search for services of a specific type, and show to display the definition of a service type.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameters are basically configuration values for a node, in other words setting or variables.

  • They are stored
    • int
    • float
    • string
    • bool
    • list
  • Each node has it's own parameters

Common commands for parameters are: 

ros2 param get <node_name> <parameter_name>
Which prints the value 
ros2 param set <node_name> <parameter_name> <value>
Which sets the value 
ros2 param dump <node_name>
Which dumps all parameters to a yaml file 
ros2 param load <node_name> <file_name>
Which loads parameters from a yaml file

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
They are tasks that require time such as moving. They offer a progress report which you can check and cancel if needed.

THey have three main characteristics: - Goal: what you want to achieve - Feedback: progress report - Result: final outcome(success/failure)

Same as in others we can use list, type, info, show, echo to get more information about actions. As well as send_goal to send a goal to an action server, and cancel_goal to cancel a goal.

ros2 action send_goal <action_name> <goal_parameters> <value>
<- Install ROS ROS2 Tools ->

docs.title: Ros2 Tools
docs.text: For ROS2 we will use a lot of command line tools, so it's important to get familiar with them, and how to work it faster. First if we tab complete (double tab) after ros2 we can see all the available commands. We can also get help for any command using -h or --help after the command, and finally we can use auto-completion for any command by pressing tab after writing part of the command.

docs.title: Colcon
docs.text: Colcon (collective construction) is a command-line tool for building, testing, and installing multiple software packages, especially popular in the Robot Operating System (ROS 2) ecosystem, automating complex workflows by handling dependencies, ordering, and environment setup for packages within a workspace, making it easier to manage projects with many interconnected components.

docs.title: Rqt
docs.text:
RQt (ROS Qt-based GUI Framework) is a framework for buildin and running graphical tools to visualize, debug and interact with ROS systems.

It should be installed by default with ROS2, and can be run with:

rqt

helping visualize topics.

To test it we will use a a basic example with turtlesim. First, in one terminal run:

ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node

Then, in another terminal run:

rqt_graph

Look at what's appearing.

Now let's run another node to control the turtle. In another terminal run:

ros2 run turtlesim turtle_teleop_key

Refresh rqt and should be able to see both nodes and the topics.

<- ROS2 Concepts ROS2 First Program ->

docs.title: First Program in ROS 2
docs.text:
We will start with our first program in ROS 2.

To implement programs, the normal workflow is:

  1. Create the workspace directory
  2. Create a package inside the src folder
  3. Implement a node
    1. Create a node
    2. Create a publisher/client/etc
    3. add parameters if needed
  4. Create a launch file
  5. Build the workspace
  6. Source the workspace
  7. Run the nodes
  8. Verify

docs.title: Create a workspace and package
docs.text:
We will start by creating a ROS2 workspace. A workspace is a directory where we can build and store our ROS2 packages. The basic Layout is as follows:

your_workspace_name/
 ├── src/
    ├── your_package_name/

A workspace can contain multiple packages, but for this example we will create a single package.

To create the workspace, open a terminal and go with the following steps.

  1. Create the workspace directory and the src folder inside it:

    mkdir -p workspace_name/src
    - mkdir means make directory - -p means create parent directories if they do not exist.

  2. Then, navigate to the workspace:

    cd workspace_name/src

  3. create an empty package:

    ros2 pkg create <package_name> --build-type ament_python --dependencies rclpy

    This will create a package for python with the name <package_name> and with the dependency rclpy, which is the ROS 2 client library for Python.

  4. Open VS Code from src folder:

    code .

  5. Here we would modify and create the files for our package. We we will do this later.

  6. We go back to our terminal and navigate to the workspace root

    cd ..

  7. Build the workspace with colcon:

    colcon build
    optionally we can --packages-select <package_name> to build only a specific package, if not it will build all packages in the workspace.

    Note

    If you have not sourced ROS 2 in your terminal, you will need to do it before building the workspace:

    source install/setup.bash

    also you can source colcon autocompletion if it's not working:

    /usr/share/colcon_argcomplete/hook/colcon-argcomplete.bash

    Finally there's an option to run colcon with --symlink-install which will create symlinks to the source files instead of copying them to the install folder. This is useful for development as you don't need to rebuild the package every time you make a change. Make sure that the python files are executable with chmod +x <file_name>.py.

docs.title: Create a Node
docs.text:
We have created and built our package, but we have not implemented any functionality yet. Let's create a simple node template to work with.

We will open again VS Code in our source folder, an then create a new python file inside the package folder, remember that the structure is like this: 

src/
 ├── your_package_name/
        ├── your_package_name/
               ├── __init__.py
               ├── your_node.py  <--- create this file

docs.title: Minimal Node
docs.text:
1. We will add an interpreter line, this will say we are using python3 to run this script in case anything tries to run it directly.

    #!/usr/bin/env python3
    2. We will add the rclpy library and import the Node class from it. 
    import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
    3. Create a main function where we initialize and shutdown at minimum. 
    def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args) # Initialize rclpy

    rclpy.shutdown()      # Shutdown rclpy
    4. Create the node, and add actions to it

        node = Node("node_name")  # Create the node with the name "node_name"
    node.get_logger().info("Node has been started, hello Node")  # Log info message
    5. Finally, we add the standard python main check to run the main function

    if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
    Here's the complete code: 
    #!/usr/bin/env python3

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args) # Initialize rclpy
    node = Node("node_name")  # Create the node with the name "node_name"
    node.get_logger().info("Node has been started, hello Node")  # Log info message
    rclpy.shutdown()      # Shutdown rclpy

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

make sure to save the file.

Let's go back to the terminal. Using the cd command navigate to the node file folder, where we can run the node, and make it executable.

cd ~/workspace_name/src/your_package_name/your_package_name
chmod +x your_node.py
you can check if it's executable with ls which will show the file executable in a different color. Which we will run next just by invoking it's name as it's executable.

./your_node.py
You can see the log message printed in the terminal, once. Let's modify our node to keep it running. We will add a loop to keep the node alive until we shut it down. After the log message, we will add a spin command to keep the node running.

rclpy.spin(node)  # Keep the node running

Now we want to install the package so we can run it from anywhere. We need to modify the setup.py file in the package folder. Open the setup.py file and add an entry point for our node in the entry_points section. Like this:

entry_points={
        'console_scripts': [
            # add this line which is <executable_name> = <package_name><file_name>:<function_name>
            "my_node = my_py_pkg.my_node:main" 
    },
save the file, go back to the terminal, navigate to the workspace root ( YOU NEVER BUILD IN SRC YOU BUILD IN THE ROOT OF THE WORKSPACE ) and build again with colcon build.

We will need to source the workspace again to make the new package available:

source install/setup.bash
or add it to your ~/.bashrc file to source it automatically every time you open a terminal:

source ~/workspace_name/install/setup.bash

Now we can run our node from anywhere using ros2 run:

ros2 run your_package_name your_node.py

With this you have created a simple ROS 2 node in Python, built it, and run it. Let's improve it my adding OOP concepts, and make it into a real template for future nodes.

docs.title: OOP Node Template
docs.text:
Instead of having everything in the main function, we will create a class that inherits from Node. This way we can encapsulate all the functionality of the node inside a class.

Let's start creating a class that inherits from Node:

class MyNode(Node):#We can name the class whatever we want, for example in a temperature sensor node we can name it TemperatureSensorNode
    def __init__(self):#We initialize the class, self refers to the instance of the class
        super().__init__("py_test") # Replaces the node creation in main
        self.get_logger().info("Node has been started, hello Node")

Now we modify the main function to create an instance of the class and spin it:

def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args) # Initialize rclpy
    my_node = MyNode()  # Create an instance of the MyNode class
    rclpy.spin(my_node)  # Keep the node running
    rclpy.shutdown()      # Shutdown rclpy

Remember to save, build and source after every change.

docs.title: Timer Function
docs.text:
We will add a timer to our node that will print a message every second. First let's create a callback function that will be called by the timer inside the class:

def timer_callback(self):
    self.get_logger().info("Timer callback called")

In our class, we will use the create_timer method to create a timer.

class MyNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("py_test")
        self.get_logger().info("Node has been started, hello Node")
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback)  # Create a timer that calls timer_callback every 1 second

Test it by saving, building, sourcing and running the node again. You should see the timer callback message every second.

Let's go a little further and add a counter that increments every time the timer callback is called.

in our initializer, we will add a counter variable:

class MyNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("py_test") 
        self.get_logger().info("Node has been started, hello Node")
        self.counter=0 # Initialize counter
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.timer_callback)
and modify the timer callback to increment and print the counter:

def timer_callback(self):
        self.get_logger().info("Timer callback called" + str(self.counter))
        self.counter += 1

docs.title: Create a Topic
docs.text: We will use our template to create a publisher and subscriber. Let's duplicate our node file and name it template.py. Just so that we have a clean template to work with in the future. We will duplicate it again and name it my_publisher.py and my_subscriber.py for our publisher and subscriber nodes.

docs.title: Write a Publisher
docs.text:
Inside our main class during initialization we will create a publisher. A publisher needs a topic name, a message type and a queue size. Because of this let's check what message types are available in ROS 2. We can check the available message types with the following command:

ros2 interface show example_interfaces/msg/String

we can see that the String message type has a single field called data of type string. We will use this message type for our publisher. So we'll import it:

from example_interfaces.msg import String

before going further, we added a new impor which means we need to add a new dependency to our package. Open the package.xml file and add the following line inside the <depend> tags:

<depend>example_interfaces</depend>
Now we can create the publisher in our class initializer:

class myPublisher(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("my_publisher")
                                              #(type, topic name, queue size)
        self._publisher = self.create_publisher(String, "robot_talk", 10)

THis publisher wont do anything yet, so let's create a method that will publish a message every second using a timer. 

def talk(self):
        msg = String()
        msg.data = "Hello"
        self.publisher_.publish(msg)
This method creates a String message, sets its data(remember it's data because it inherited from the interfaces.msg which had a data field) to "Hello" and publishes it. Now we will create a timer that calls this method every second and a log message that publisher has started.

def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("my_publisher")
        self.publisher_ = self.create_publisher(String, "robot_talk", 10)
        self.create_timer(1.0, self.talk)
        self.get_logger().info("My robot is talking on a topic")
we can test it by saving, building, sourcing and running the publisher node. You should see the log message once, but nothing else will happen because we don't have any subscribers yet. we can verify that the topic is being published with:

 ros2 node info /my_publisher
which will show the topics being published by the node, or: 
    ros2 topic list
which will show all topics being published in the system, you should see robot_talk in the list, or finally you can use: 
    ros2 topic echo /robot_talk
which will print the messages being published on the topic.

docs.title: Write a Subscriber
docs.text:
We have our publisher, now let's create a subscriber that listens to the robot_talk topic. We will create a new file called my_subscriber.py and implement the subscriber node there.

We will import the same message type as the publisher, and create a method for a callback that will be called when a message is received.

def callback_receive_info(self, msg: String): #its receiving a msg of type String
        self.get_logger().info(msg.data) #print the data field

Now we create the subscriber in the class initializer:

def __init__(self):
    super().__init__("Listener") 
    self.subscriber = self.create_subscription(
        String,"robot_talk", self.callback_receive_info,10)
       # type, topic name, callback function, queue size

Before building, remember to add the console script entry point in the setup.py file. 

 entry_points={
        'console_scripts': [
            "my_node = my_py_pkg.my_node:main",
            "my_talk = my_py_pkg.my_publisher:main",
            "my_listen = my_py_pkg.my_subscriber:main"
        ],
    },

Now we can save, build, source and run the subscriber node in a new terminal. If we have the publisher running, we should see the messages being printed in the subscriber terminal.

Now before finishing lets try running multiple publishers and one subscriber, by renaming from the terminal the publisher node to my_talk_1, my_talk_2, etc. and see how the subscriber receives messages from both publishers, in your terminal run:

ros2 run my_py_pkg my_talk --ros-args -r __node:=my_talk1
and in another terminal run:

ros2 run my_py_pkg my_talk --ros-args -r __node:=my_talk2
You should see messages from both publishers in the subscriber terminal, this is because we are forcing the node name to be different for each publisher using the -r __node:=<new_name> argument.

r mean remap, and __node is a special argument that allows us to change the node name at runtime. We can even remap topics this way if needed. For example: 

ros2 run my_py_pkg my_talk --ros-args -r robot_talk:=robot_chatter

docs.title: ROS 2 Jazzy — Create a Service Server
docs.text:
In this lesson you will create a service server in ROS 2 Jazzy using Python (rclpy).

We will implement a server that receives two integers (a, b) and returns their sum (sum) using the already-installed interface:

  • example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts

docs.title: 1) Understand the service interface
docs.text:
Inspect the interface:

ros2 interface show example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts

Expected output:

int64 a
int64 b
---
int64 sum

The --- separates:

  • Request (client → server): a, b
  • Response (server → client): sum

docs.title: 2) Server implementation
docs.text: Below is the same server code, but divided into sections so each part is easier to understand.

docs.title: Imports
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
# Service interface (srv, not msg)
from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts

What this does

  • Services live under ...srv (not ...msg).
  • AddTwoInts contains both:
    • AddTwoInts.Request (fields: a, b)
    • AddTwoInts.Response (field: sum)

docs.title: Define the node class and constructor
docs.text:
class AddTwoIntsServerNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("add_two_ints_server")

What this does

  • Creates a node class named AddTwoIntsServerNode
  • Sets the node name to add_two_ints_server

docs.title: Create the service server
docs.text:
Inside the constructor, we create the service server:

        # Create the service server: (type, service_name, callback)
        self._server = self.create_service(
            AddTwoInts, # service type
            "add_two_ints", # service name
            self.callback_add_two_ints, # callback function
        )

        self.get_logger().info("AddTwoInts service server has been started.")

Parameters explained

  • Type: AddTwoInts (the service interface)
  • Service name: "add_two_ints"
  • Recommend using a verb for services (actions or computations): enable_motor, compute_ik, add_two_ints
  • Callback: self.callback_add_two_ints
  • This runs whenever a client calls the service.

docs.title: The service callback (request → response)
docs.text:
In our node class, we define the callback function that processes incoming service calls:

    def callback_add_two_ints(self, request: AddTwoInts.Request, response: AddTwoInts.Response):
        # Compute result
        response.sum = request.a + request.b

        # Log for visibility
        self.get_logger().info(f"{request.a} + {request.b} = {response.sum}")

        # IMPORTANT: you must return the response in Python
        return response

What this does

  • request contains incoming fields: request.a, request.b
  • response is the object you must fill: response.sum = ...
  • Critical: In Python service servers, you must return response If you forget to return it, the node runs but service calls will fail at runtime.

docs.title: The main() function (init → spin → shutdown)
docs.text:
Same as usual, we have a main() function to run the node, which initializes ROS, creates the node, spins it, and shuts down cleanly.

def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = AddTwoIntsServerNode()
    rclpy.spin(node)
    rclpy.shutdown()

docs.title: 3) Full code (complete file)
docs.text:
Below is the full server file exactly as you should keep it.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

# Service interface (srv, not msg)
from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts


class AddTwoIntsServerNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("add_two_ints_server")

        # Create the service server: (type, service_name, callback)
        self._server = self.create_service(
            AddTwoInts,
            "add_two_ints",
            self.callback_add_two_ints,
        )

        self.get_logger().info("AddTwoInts service server has been started.")

    def callback_add_two_ints(self, request: AddTwoInts.Request, response: AddTwoInts.Response):
        # Compute result
        response.sum = request.a + request.b

        # Log for visibility
        self.get_logger().info(f"{request.a} + {request.b} = {response.sum}")

        # IMPORTANT: you must return the response in Python
        return response


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = AddTwoIntsServerNode()
    rclpy.spin(node)
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 4) Test quickly from terminal
docs.text:
Before testing, make sure you have done the following:

  • Added example_interfaces as a dependency in your package.xml.
  • Added an entry point for the server script in your setup.py.

With the server running:

ros2 run my_py_pkg add_two_ints_server

Call it:

ros2 service call /add_two_ints example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts "{a: 3, b: 7}"

docs.title: ROS 2 Jazzy — Create a Service Client
docs.text:
In this lesson you will create a service client in ROS 2 Jazzy using Python (rclpy).

We will call the service:

  • Interface: example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts
  • Service name: /add_two_ints

docs.title: Imports
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

from functools import partial

from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts

What this does

  • partial lets us pass extra arguments into a callback cleanly.
  • AddTwoInts is the service type:
  • AddTwoInts.Request has a, b
  • AddTwoInts.Response has sum

docs.title: Define the client node class
docs.text:
class AddTwoIntsClientNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("add_two_ints_client")

What this does - Creates a node named add_two_ints_client

docs.title: Create the service client
docs.text:
Inside the constructor:

        self._client = self.create_client(
            AddTwoInts, # service type
            "add_two_ints") # service name (must match server)

Parameters

  • Type: AddTwoInts which we imported from example_interfaces.srv
  • Service name: "add_two_ints" (must match the server) which comes from the server code we wrote in the previous lesson

docs.title: Method to send requests
docs.text:
Inside the class, add:

    def call_add_two_ints(self, a: int, b: int):
        # Wait for service (safe startup)
        while not self._client.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0):
            self.get_logger().warn("Service '/add_two_ints' not available, waiting...")
        # Build request
        request = AddTwoInts.Request()
        request.a = a
        request.b = b

        # Send async request
        # Creates a Future that will eventually hold the response
        future = self._client.call_async(request)

        # Register callback; pass request too (so we can log a + b)
        # This wont run immediately — it runs when the response arrives
        future.add_done_callback(partial(self.callback_call_add_two_ints, request))

What this does

  1. Wait until the server is available (safe startup)
  2. Build a request object, initializing a and b
  3. Send the request asynchronously (call_async)
  4. Register a callback that will run when the response arrives

Why async?

  • call() can block and cause deadlocks in typical ROS node patterns.
  • call_async() + callbacks works cleanly with rclpy.spin(node).

Future and callbacks

  • A Future is a placeholder for a result that will arrive later (the response).
  • When a response arrives, the callback we registered will be called with the Future, allowing us to extract the response.

docs.title: Response callback
docs.text:
# Callback for when the future completes (response received)
    def callback_call_add_two_ints(self, request: AddTwoInts.Request, future):
        response = future.result()
        self.get_logger().info(f"{request.a} + {request.b} = {response.sum}")

What this does

  • Extracts the response from the future
  • Logs the full equation (we can do this because we passed request using partial)

docs.title: Example usage (send multiple requests)
docs.text:
self.call_add_two_ints(2, 7)
        self.call_add_two_ints(1, 4)
        self.call_add_two_ints(10, 20)

What this demonstrates

  • One client can send many requests
  • Responses will arrive and trigger the callback each time

docs.title: main() (init → spin → shutdown)
docs.text:
def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = AddTwoIntsClientNode()
    rclpy.spin(node)
    rclpy.shutdown()

docs.title: 2) Full code
docs.text:
Create: my_py_pkg/add_two_ints_client.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

from functools import partial

from example_interfaces.srv import AddTwoInts


class AddTwoIntsClientNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("add_two_ints_client")

        # Create client once
        self._client = self.create_client(AddTwoInts, "add_two_ints")

        # Example calls (send multiple requests)
        self.call_add_two_ints(2, 7)
        self.call_add_two_ints(1, 4)
        self.call_add_two_ints(10, 20)

    def call_add_two_ints(self, a: int, b: int):
        # Wait for service (safe startup)
        while not self._client.wait_for_service(timeout_sec=1.0):
            self.get_logger().warn("Service '/add_two_ints' not available, waiting...")

        # Build request
        request = AddTwoInts.Request()
        request.a = a
        request.b = b

        # Send async request
        future = self._client.call_async(request)

        # Register callback; pass request too (so we can log a + b)
        future.add_done_callback(partial(self.callback_call_add_two_ints, request))

    def callback_call_add_two_ints(self, request: AddTwoInts.Request, future):
        # Extract response
        response = future.result()
        self.get_logger().info(f"{request.a} + {request.b} = {response.sum}")


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = AddTwoIntsClientNode()
    rclpy.spin(node)
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 3) Register the executable in setup.py
docs.text:
Add:

entry_points={
    "console_scripts": [
        "add_two_ints_client = my_py_pkg.add_two_ints_client:main",
    ],
},

docs.title: 4) Build and run
docs.text:
Build with symlink install:

cd ~/your_ws
colcon build 
source install/setup.bash

Terminal A (server):

ros2 run my_py_pkg add_two_ints_server

Terminal B (client):

ros2 run my_py_pkg add_two_ints_client

Expected logs: - Server prints each received request - Client prints: 2 + 7 = 9, 1 + 4 = 5, 10 + 20 = 30

docs.title: Change it to ask the user for input
docs.text:
Let's modify the client so it asks the user for two integers in the terminal, then sends the request.

If you want your client to ask the user for numbers in the terminal, you should not put a while rclpy.ok(): input(...) loop inside __init__(). A loop with input() blocks the constructor forever, so your program may never reach:

rclpy.spin(node)

Without spinning, ROS 2 may not process incoming service responses, meaning your future done-callback may not run reliably.

Instead, we will use the threading module to run a separate thread that handles user input.

First import threading at the top:

import threading

Then, in the constructor, start a new thread that runs a method to handle user input:

        # Start a separate thread for user input
        threading.Thread(target=self.user_input_loop, daemon=True).start()
Finally create the user_input_loop method that runs in the separate thread:

def user_input_loop(self):
    while rclpy.ok():
        try:
            a = int(input("Enter first integer (a): "))
            b = int(input("Enter second integer (b): "))
            self.call_add_two_ints(a, b)
        except ValueError:
            print("Please enter valid integers.")
        except (KeyboardInterrupt, EOFError):
            print("Exiting client.")
            break

docs.title: ROS2 Jazzy — Custom Interface Message
docs.text:
In this lesson you will create your first custom ROS 2 interface by defining a custom message (.msg) and building it so it becomes available.

We will create:

  • Package: my_robot_interfaces
  • Message: msg/HardwareStatus.msg

This message will represent a simple “robot hardware status” payload (temperature, readiness flag, debug string).

docs.title: 1) Where should custom interfaces live?
docs.text:
Technically, you can place message/service definitions in many packages.

In practice, it is much cleaner to put all custom interfaces in one dedicated package, for example:

  • my_robot_interfaces

Why this helps:

  • Avoids dependency chaos later
  • Other packages only need one dependency: the interface package
  • Your app becomes easier to scale and maintain

You only create the interface package once. After that, adding a new interface is just: create file → add it to CMake → build.

docs.title: 2) Create an interface package
docs.text:
From your ROS 2 workspace src/ folder:

cd ~/your_ws/src
ros2 pkg create my_robot_interfaces

Naming recommendation:

  • Use your application/robot name + _interfaces
  • Example: ackerman_interfaces, ibero_robot_interfaces, abc_interfaces

After creation you will see a typical CMake package structure:

my_robot_interfaces/
  CMakeLists.txt
  package.xml
  include/        (not needed for interfaces)
  src/            (not needed for interfaces)

docs.title: Clean up the package (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
Remove folders you will not use:

cd my_robot_interfaces
rm -rf include src

Now the package is minimal:

my_robot_interfaces/
  CMakeLists.txt
  package.xml

docs.title: 3) Configure package.xml (required lines)
docs.text:
Open my_robot_interfaces/package.xml and add three lines required for rosidl interface generation:

<buildtool_depend>rosidl_default_generators</buildtool_depend>
<exec_depend>rosidl_default_runtime</exec_depend>
<member_of_group>rosidl_interface_packages</member_of_group>

A typical placement is right after the existing ament_cmake dependency.

Result (snippet example): 

<buildtool_depend>ament_cmake</buildtool_depend>

<buildtool_depend>rosidl_default_generators</buildtool_depend>
<exec_depend>rosidl_default_runtime</exec_depend>
<member_of_group>rosidl_interface_packages</member_of_group>

docs.title: 4) Configure CMakeLists.txt
docs.text:
Open my_robot_interfaces/CMakeLists.txt.

You need three key parts:

1) Find generators 2) Generate interfaces 3) Export runtime dependencies

Go from this (default):

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.8)
project(my_robot_interfaces)

if(CMAKE_COMPILER_IS_GNUCXX OR CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "Clang")
  add_compile_options(-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)
endif()

# find dependencies
find_package(ament_cmake REQUIRED)
# uncomment the following section in order to fill in
# further dependencies manually.
# find_package(<dependency> REQUIRED)

if(BUILD_TESTING)
  find_package(ament_lint_auto REQUIRED)
  # the following line skips the linter which checks for copyrights
  # comment the line when a copyright and license is added to all source files
  set(ament_cmake_copyright_FOUND TRUE)
  # the following line skips cpplint (only works in a git repo)
  # comment the line when this package is in a git repo and when
  # a copyright and license is added to all source files
  set(ament_cmake_cpplint_FOUND TRUE)
  ament_lint_auto_find_test_dependencies()
endif()

ament_package()

to this, were we added a few dependencies and the interface generation block:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.8)
project(my_robot_interfaces)

if(CMAKE_COMPILER_IS_GNUCXX OR CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "Clang")
  add_compile_options(-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic)
endif()

# find dependencies
find_package(ament_cmake REQUIRED)
find_package(rosidl_default_generators REQUIRED)

rosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME}

)

ament_export_dependencies(rosidl_default_runtime)

ament_package()

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Put one interface per line inside rosidl_generate_interfaces(...)
  • No commas between lines
  • Paths are relative to the package root (e.g., msg/HardwareStatus.msg)

docs.title: 5) Create your first message
docs.text:
Inside my_robot_interfaces/, create the message folder:

mkdir -p msg

Create the message file:

touch msg/HardwareStatus.msg

and add it to CMakeLists.txt:

rosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME}
  "msg/HardwareStatus.msg"
)

docs.title: Naming rules
docs.text:
For interface files:

  • Use UpperCamelCase (start uppercase, each word starts uppercase)
  • No underscores, no dashes in the filename
  • Don’t include redundant words like “Message”

docs.title: 6) Define message fields
docs.text:
Edit msg/HardwareStatus.msg:

float64 temperature
bool are_motors_ready
string debug_message

docs.title: Rules for fields
docs.text:
• One field per line
  • Format: <type> <name>
  • Use underscores for multiword field names (snake_case)
  • No commas or punctuation

Primitive types used here:

  • float64
  • bool
  • string

docs.title: 7) Build the interface package
docs.text:
Go to the workspace root (not inside src/):

cd ~/your_ws
colcon build --packages-select my_robot_interfaces

The first build that generates interfaces can take longer than usual.

Then source your workspace, as we created a new package with new interfaces:

source install/setup.bash

If you open a new terminal later, you must source again. Unless you have added the source line to your ~/.bashrc .

docs.title: 8) Verify the interface exists
docs.text:
Use ros2 interface show to confirm your message is discoverable:

ros2 interface show my_robot_interfaces/msg/HardwareStatus

Expected output:

float64 temperature
bool are_motors_ready
string debug_message

docs.title: 9) Publish your custom message
docs.text:
Now we will modify our template node to publish messages of type:

  • my_robot_interfaces/msg/HardwareStatus

docs.title: 1) Add the dependency to your Python package
docs.text:
Edit your Python package package.xml (example: my_py_pkg/package.xml) and add:

<depend>my_robot_interfaces</depend>

docs.title: 2) Modify the template node to publish HardwareStatus
docs.text:
Add the import:

from my_robot_interfaces.msg import HardwareStatus

Create a publisher in __init__():

self.publisher_ = self.create_publisher(HardwareStatus, "hardware_status", 10)

Create a timer:

self.timer_ = self.create_timer(0.5, self.publish_status)

Add the publish method:

def publish_status(self):
    msg = HardwareStatus()
    msg.temperature = 36.5
    msg.are_motors_ready = True
    msg.debug_message = "OK"

    self.publisher_.publish(msg)

docs.title: 3) Full updated template node
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

from my_robot_interfaces.msg import HardwareStatus


class MyNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("py_test")

        # Publisher using the custom message type
        self.publisher_ = self.create_publisher(HardwareStatus, "hardware_status", 10)

        # Publish at 2 Hz
        self.timer_ = self.create_timer(0.5, self.publish_status)

    def publish_status(self):
        msg = HardwareStatus()
        msg.temperature = 36.5
        msg.are_motors_ready = True
        msg.debug_message = "OK"

        self.publisher_.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    my_node = MyNode()
    rclpy.spin(my_node)
    rclpy.shutdown()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

source install/setup.bash

ros2 topic echo /hardware_status

docs.title: ROS 2 Jazzy — Custom Service Interface
docs.text:
You will:

1) Create a custom service interface: ComputeRectangleArea.srv 2) Build it in my_robot_interfaces 3) Use it in a Python service server based on your template node

docs.title: 1) Create the custom service interface
docs.text:
Inside your interface package:

cd ~/your_ws/src/my_robot_interfaces
mkdir -p srv
touch srv/ComputeRectangleArea.srv

Edit srv/ComputeRectangleArea.srv:

float64 length
float64 width
---
float64 area

docs.title: Register it in CMakeLists.txt
docs.text:
Open my_robot_interfaces/CMakeLists.txt and add the file path:

rosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME}
  "msg/HardwareStatus.msg"
  "srv/ComputeRectangleArea.srv"
)

Build and source:

cd ~/your_ws
colcon build --packages-select my_robot_interfaces
source install/setup.bash

Verify:

ros2 interface show my_robot_interfaces/srv/ComputeRectangleArea

docs.title: 2.1 Add dependency in your Python package
docs.text:
In your Python package package.xml (example: my_py_pkg/package.xml), add:

<depend>my_robot_interfaces</depend>

docs.title: 3) Python service server using the template node
docs.text:
We will start from your node template from your first program section.

And we will add:

  • the import for the custom service type
  • create_service(...)
  • a callback that computes area = length * width

docs.title: Import the custom service type
docs.text: from my_robot_interfaces.srv import ComputeRectangleArea

docs.title: Create the service server in __init__()
docs.text:
self.server_ = self.create_service(
    ComputeRectangleArea,
    "compute_rectangle_area",
    self.cb_compute_rectangle_area,
)

docs.title: Implement the callback
docs.text:
def cb_compute_rectangle_area(self, request, response):
    response.area = request.length * request.width
    self.get_logger().info(
        f"length={request.length}, width={request.width} -> area={response.area}"
    )
    return response

Reminder: in Python service servers you must return the response.

docs.title: 4) Full server code with the custom service
docs.text:
Create a new file in your Python package, for example:

  • my_py_pkg/compute_rectangle_area_server.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

from my_robot_interfaces.srv import ComputeRectangleArea


class MyNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("compute_rectangle_area_server")

        self.server_ = self.create_service(
            ComputeRectangleArea,
            "compute_rectangle_area",
            self.cb_compute_rectangle_area,
        )

        self.get_logger().info("ComputeRectangleArea service server started.")

    def cb_compute_rectangle_area(self, request, response):
        response.area = request.length * request.width

        self.get_logger().info(
            f"length={request.length}, width={request.width} -> area={response.area}"
        )

        return response


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    my_node = MyNode()
    rclpy.spin(my_node)
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: ROS 2 Jazzy — Parameters in Python Nodes
docs.text:
In this lesson you will add parameters to an existing Python node (the number publisher) so you can change behavior at runtime without modifying code or rebuilding.

We will convert two hard-coded values into parameters:

  • number (integer): the value to publish
  • timer_period (float): how often to publish (seconds)

docs.title: Parameter Concept
docs.text:
We will use a publisher code to show the concepto we already know the structure:

  • A publisher
  • A timer
  • Publish a number periodically

Before parameters, the node usually contains hard-coded values like:

  • number = 2
  • timer period = 1.0 s

Problem:

  • If we wanted a different number or frequency, you must edit code (and often rebuild).

Solution:

  • Use parameters.

docs.title: Parameters in Python are a 2-step process
docs.text:
For each parameter:

1) Declare it (name + default value) 2) Get its current value (then use it in your code)

docs.title: Why declare first?
docs.text:
Declaring registers the parameter in the node so:

  • it appears in ros2 param list
  • it can be overridden from the terminal
  • its type is established (based on the default value)

docs.title: Add parameters in the constructor
docs.text:
Add these lines near the top of your node __init__() (before publishers/timers):

# 1) Declare parameters (name, default_value)
self.declare_parameter("number", 2)          # int (type inferred from default)
self.declare_parameter("timer_period", 1.0)  # float (type inferred from default)

# 2) Get parameter values (IMPORTANT: .value is a property, not a method)
self.number_ = self.get_parameter("number").value
self.timer_period_ = self.get_parameter("timer_period").value

docs.title: Use the parameters in your publisher/timer
docs.text:
Now replace hard-coded values:

  • Publish self.number_ instead of 2
  • Create timer using self.timer_period_ instead of 1.0

Example:

self.timer_ = self.create_timer(self.timer_period_, self.timer_callback)

And inside the callback:

msg.data = self.number_
self.publisher_.publish(msg)

docs.title: Full example node
docs.text:
This version publishes std_msgs/msg/Int64 on topic /number.

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import Int64


class NumberPublisher(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("number_publisher")

        # ---- Parameters (declare -> get) ----
        self.declare_parameter("number", 2)
        self.declare_parameter("timer_period", 1.0)

        self.number_ = self.get_parameter("number").value
        self.timer_period_ = self.get_parameter("timer_period").value

        # ---- Publisher + timer ----
        self.publisher_ = self.create_publisher(Int64, "number", 10)
        self.timer_ = self.create_timer(self.timer_period_, self.timer_callback)

        self.get_logger().info(
            f"Started number_publisher with number={self.number_}, timer_period={self.timer_period_}"
        )

    def timer_callback(self):
        msg = Int64()
        msg.data = int(self.number_)  # ensure int for Int64
        self.publisher_.publish(msg)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = NumberPublisher()
    rclpy.spin(node)
    rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
Build your Python package:

cd ~/your_ws
colcon build --packages-select my_py_pkg
source install/setup.bash

Run normally:

ros2 run my_py_pkg number_publisher

Expected behavior: - Publishes 2 every 1.0 seconds

docs.title: Inspect parameters from the terminal
docs.text:
While the node is running:

ros2 param list

You should see your node parameters, for example:

  • /number_publisher.number
  • /number_publisher.timer_period

docs.title: Override parameters at runtime
docs.text:
Stop the node and run again, but override values:

ros2 run my_py_pkg number_publisher --ros-args -p number:=3 -p timer_period:=0.5

Expected behavior: - Publishes 3 every 0.5 seconds

Override only one parameter:

ros2 run my_py_pkg number_publisher --ros-args -p number:=3

Expected behavior: - Publishes 3 every 1.0 seconds (timer_period default still used)

docs.title: Verify publishing
docs.text:
In another terminal:

ros2 topic echo /number

You should see the number changing based on parameters.

docs.title: YAML parameter files
docs.text:
We could create a YAML File and load the parameters at runtime.

Why this matters: - A real node can have dozens of parameters. - Passing many -p name:=value arguments in the terminal becomes slow and error-prone. - YAML lets you save multiple configurations and reuse them easily.

In the next section (launch files), you will typically install YAML files inside the workspace and load them from launch. For now, you can place them anywhere (e.g., your home directory).

docs.title: Create a folder for YAML parameter files
docs.text:
Example (any location is fine for now):

mkdir -p ~/yaml_params

Create a file:

touch ~/yaml_params/number_params.yaml

docs.title: YAML structure (single node)
docs.text:
A ROS 2 params YAML file uses this structure:

  • Top level key = node name
  • Inside: ros__parameters:
  • Inside: list of parameters as name: value

Example for a node named /number_publisher:

number_publisher:
  ros__parameters:
    number: 5
    timer_period: 0.7

docs.title: Critical rules
docs.text:
• Node name must match exactly.
  • Indentation matters (use spaces, commonly 2 spaces per level).
  • Parameter values must match the type declared in code.

docs.title: Run the node using the YAML file
docs.text:
Instead of many -p flags, run:

ros2 run my_py_pkg number_publisher --ros-args --params-file ~/yaml_params/number_params.yaml

Verify:

ros2 topic echo /number

You should see 5 published, and the timing should reflect timer_period: 0.7.

If you want to check the publish rate:

ros2 topic hz /number

(If the period is 0.7, the frequency is about 1 / 0.7 ≈ 1.4 Hz.)

docs.title: YAML structure (multiple nodes in one file)
docs.text:
A single YAML file can contain parameter sets for many nodes.

Example:

number_publisher_one:
  ros__parameters:
    number: 5
    timer_period: 0.7

number_publisher_two:
  ros__parameters:
    number: 3
    timer_period: 1.0

How it works: - When a node starts with --params-file ..., it checks: - “Is there an entry in this YAML matching my node name?” - If yes → it loads that parameter block. - If no → it ignores the file (node uses default parameter values).

docs.title: Run two nodes with different configs (same YAML)
Start Node 1 (rename to match YAML)
docs.text: ros2 run my_py_pkg number_publisher   --ros-args -r __node:=number_publisher_one   --params-file ~/yaml_params/number_params.yaml

docs.title: Start Node 2 (rename to match YAML)
docs.text: ros2 run my_py_pkg number_publisher   --ros-args -r __node:=number_publisher_two   --params-file ~/yaml_params/number_params.yaml

docs.title: Verify both are publishing
docs.text:
ros2 topic echo /number

You should see values from both nodes (e.g., 5 and 3) arriving at different rates.

docs.title: ROS 2 Jazzy — Launch Files
docs.text:
In this lesson you will create a dedicated bringup package to store:

  • Launch files (launch/)
  • Configuration files (config/) YAML parameter files

Then you will create an XML launch file that starts multiple nodes, and you will set parameters:

1) Inline in the launch file 2) From a YAML file installed with the bringup package

docs.title: Create a dedicated bringup package
docs.text:
From your workspace src/ folder:

cd ~/your_ws/src
ros2 pkg create my_robot_bringup

Why this package exists:

  • You keep launch files + configs in one place
  • Cleaner dependencies and project structure

docs.title: Clean up folders you do not need
docs.text:
cd my_robot_bringup
rm -rf include src
mkdir -p launch
mkdir -p config

Your bringup package should look like:

my_robot_bringup/
  package.xml
  CMakeLists.txt
  launch/
  config/

docs.title: Install launch/ and config/ folders (CMake)
docs.text:
Open my_robot_bringup/CMakeLists.txt and keep it minimal.

Between find_package(...) and ament_package() add:

install(DIRECTORY
  launch
  config
  DESTINATION share/${PROJECT_NAME}/
)

This installs both folders into:

~/your_ws/install/my_robot_bringup/share/my_robot_bringup/

You only do this once. After that, any file you put inside launch/ or config/ will be installed automatically after rebuilding.

docs.title: Create your first XML launch file
docs.text:
Create:

touch launch/number_app.launch.xml

Minimal structure:

<launch>
</launch>

Everything you add goes inside the <launch> ... </launch> tags.

docs.title: Start two nodes from the launch file
docs.text:
Example application:

  • Start number_publisher
  • Start number_counter

Edit launch/number_app.launch.xml:

<launch>

  <node pkg="my_py_pkg" exec="number_publisher" />

  <node pkg="my_cpp_pkg" exec="number_counter" />

</launch>

How to think about it:

  • If you can run a node with:
  • ros2 run <pkg> <exec>
  • Then the launch node line is basically the same:
  • <node pkg="..." exec="..." />

docs.title: Add runtime dependencies in package.xml
docs.text:
Because my_robot_bringup launches executables from other packages, add them as execution dependencies.

Open my_robot_bringup/package.xml and add:

<exec_depend>my_pkg</exec_depend>

In other words, each time you reference a new package in your launch file, add it as an <exec_depend>.

docs.title: Build and run the launch file
docs.text:
Build only the bringup package:

cd ~/your_ws
colcon build --packages-select my_robot_bringup
source install/setup.bash

Launch:

ros2 launch my_robot_bringup number_app.launch.xml

Verify:

ros2 node list
ros2 topic list

docs.title: Set parameters inside the launch file
docs.text:
If your number_publisher node declares parameters (example: number, timer_period), you can set them inside its <node> tag.

Update the number_publisher node tag:

<launch>

  <node pkg="my_py_pkg" exec="number_publisher">
    <param name="number" value="6" />
    <param name="timer_period" value="1.5" />
  </node>

  <node pkg="my_cpp_pkg" exec="number_counter" />

</launch>

Notes:

  • Parameter names must match exactly what you declared in code (declare_parameter(...)).
  • Values must match the parameter type.

Verify quickly:

ros2 param get /number_publisher number
ros2 param get /number_publisher timer_period

docs.title: Install and load parameters from a YAML file
docs.text: For bigger nodes with many parameters, use YAML.

docs.title: Create a YAML file inside config/
docs.text:
Create inside my_robot_bringup/config/:

touch config/number_app.yaml

Example YAML:

number_publisher:
  ros__parameters:
    number: 6
    timer_period: 1.5

docs.title: Load the YAML file from XML launch
docs.text:
Replace the inline params with:

<launch>

  <node pkg="<pkg_name>" exec="<exec_name>">
    <param from="$(find-pkg-share my_robot_bringup)/config/<filename>.yaml" />
  </node>

</launch>

Key idea:

  • $(find-pkg-share <launch_pkg>) finds the installed path of your bringup package
  • Then you append /config/number_app.yaml

docs.title: Build and run again
docs.text:
cd ~/your_ws
colcon build --packages-select my_robot_bringup
source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch my_robot_bringup number_app.launch.xml

You should get the same parameter values, but now they come from YAML.

<- ROS2 Parameters

docs.title: Spatial Descriptions and Transformations
docs.text: In robotics, it is essential to describe the position and orientation of objects in three-dimensional space. This is typically done using coordinate frames and transformation matrices.

docs.title: Position
docs.text:
The position of a point in 3D space can be represented using a 3-dimensional vector.

  • There must be a universal reference frame (often called the "world" frame) to which all other frames are related.

  • We can find any point using a vector of position 3x1 relative to a reference frame:

\[ {}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{p}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} p_x \\ p_y \\ p_z \end{bmatrix} \]

where:

\( p_x, p_y, p_z \) are the coordinates of the point in frame B with respect to frame A.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
To describe orientation in 3D space, we use a vector of rotation.

  • To describe the orientation, we assign to the body its own frame, relative to the reference frame.
  • The new frame is described using unit vectors of its main axes (x,y,z) in terms of A.
  • By grouping them, it becomes a 3x3 rotation matrix
\[ {}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} {}^{A}\hat{X}\_B & {}^{A}\hat{Y}\_B & {}^{A}\hat{Z}\_B \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r*{12} & r*{13} \\ r*{21} & r*{22} & r*{23} \\ r*{31} & r*{32} & r*{33} \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: Transforms Math
docs.text:
• To be able to represent the behavior of a robot over time, we need to obtain functions that describe how the position and orientation change.

  • We require functions that describe movement in space, considering position and orientation, and their transformations: translation and rotation.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
A function is a mathematical relation that associates each element of a set (domain) with a unique element of another set (codomain).

Let's asume we have a function \( f(p): Ap \), where:

  • \( A \) is a \( n \times n \) matrix, and \(n\) is the number of dimensions of \( p \).
  • \( p \) is a vector of position.
  • Functions for transforms must be linear.

For example:

Identity transformation

\[ \begin{bmatrix} X_2 \\ Y_2 \end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X_1 \\ Y_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X_1 \\ Y_1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Scaling transformation

\[ \begin{bmatrix} X_2 \\ Y_2 \end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix} S_x & 0 \\ 0 & S_y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X_1 \\ Y_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} S_x X_1 \\ S_y Y_1 \end{bmatrix} \]

If we use linear functions we have a few benefits:

  • The superposition principle applies: the result of applying two functions in sequence is the same as applying a single function that is the sum of the two functions.
  • The functions can be inverted: if a function transforms a point from position A to position B
  • Linear transformations can be chained through multiplication.

docs.title: Rotation Transformations
Rotation matrices properties
docs.text:
• The inverse of a rotation matrix is equal to its transpose:
\[ {}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{R}^{-1} = {}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{R}^T \]
  • It's determinant is equal to 1:

$$ \text{det}({}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{R}) = 1 $$

  • The composition of two rotation matrices results in another rotation matrix:
\[ {}^{A}_{C}\mathbf{R} = {}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{R} \cdot {}^{B}_{C}\mathbf{R} \]
  • We follow the right-hand rule for defining the direction of rotation around an axis.

docs.title: Rotation Matrix in 3D
docs.text:
Any random rotation in 3D can be represented as a combination of three elemental rotations about the principal axes (X, Y, and Z). Called Euler angles.

We can still multiply rotation matrices to achieve combined rotations in 3D space. However, the order of multiplication matters because matrix multiplication is not commutative.

In robotics, you write vectors as columns and transform like this:

\[ v' = R v \]

Where \( v \) is the original vector, \( R \) is the rotation matrix, and \( v' \) is the rotated vector.

If you do \( R_1 \) followed by \( R_2 \), you write:

\[ v'' = R_2 (R_1 v) = (R_2 R_1) v \]

So the matrix closest to the vector happens first → right-to-left application.

As we add another dimension, the rotation matrices become more complex. Instead of having a single function for rotation, we now have three separate functions, each corresponding to a rotation about one of the principal axes (X, Y, and Z).

$$ R_z(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta) & -\sin(\theta) & 0 \\ \sin(\theta) & \cos(\theta) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ $$ R_y(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} \\ \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} \\ \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} \end{bmatrix} $$ $$ R_y(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} \\ \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} \\ \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} & \underline{\hspace{0.5cm}} \end{bmatrix} $$

docs.title: Translation Transform
docs.text:
$$ f(p) = p + b $$

Where:

  • \(p\) is the original position vector.
  • \(b\) is the translation vector.
$$ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} t_x \\ t_y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x + t_x \\ y + t_y \end{bmatrix} $$
