docs.title: What the existing service does
docs.text:
XYZServerGazbo.py exposes /ee_pose. When called it:

  1. Solves inverse kinematics using Levenberg-Marquardt numerical IK — see T0_3 — Numerical IK from DH Parameters for the full derivation.
  2. Creates one JointTrajectoryPoint with the solution angles.
  3. Sends it to /arm_controller/follow_joint_trajectory.

The controller receives that single target and interpolates on its own — you have no control over speed, acceleration, or path shape. That is the limitation this practical solves.

docs.title: Exercise 0.1 — Baseline observation
docs.text:
1. Launch the simulation and call /ee_pose to two different targets.
  2. Open PlotJuggler and plot /joint_states/velocity[0] for each move.
  3. Does the velocity profile look trapezoidal? Note your observation — you will compare this with Part 2.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: sudo apt install ros-jazzy-plotjuggler-ros

docs.title: Launch
docs.text:
Open a new terminal while the simulation is running:

ros2 run plotjuggler plotjuggler

docs.title: Connecting to the robot
docs.text:
1. Click Streaming → ROS2 Topic Subscriber → Start.
  2. Find /joint_states in the topic list.
  3. Expand it: position[0]…[5], velocity[0]…[5], effort[0]…[5].
  4. Drag signals to the plot area. Right-click a panel to split it.

docs.title: Suggested panel layout
docs.text:
Top Middle Bottom position[0]…[5] velocity[0]…[5] effort[0]…[5]

Toggle individual joints by clicking their legend entries. All panels share a time axis — use Sync to align them.

docs.title: Deriving acceleration
docs.text:
PlotJuggler computes acceleration from velocity with no code changes. Right-click any velocity signal → Apply function → ∂/∂t. The result is the numerical time-derivative, equivalent to the finite-difference acceleration described in T0_1 — Acceleration graph.

What effort means in Gazebo: the position controller applies torque proportional to position error (gain = 0.1, visible in your launch log). Effort is zero when the robot holds still. During a trapezoidal trajectory it spikes during the ramp-up and ramp-down phases — a direct visual confirmation of the T0_1 — Ramps use theory.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In XYZServerGazebo.py the robot receives a target (x, y, z), solves inverse kinematics, and sends a single waypoint to the controller. The controller then decides entirely on its own how to get there — how fast, how smooth, when to accelerate. You had no control over any of that.

In this session you will extend that node into TrajectoryServer.py, which exposes a new service /ee_traj_joint. Instead of sending one waypoint, it sends a complete sequence of time-stamped waypoints that form a trapezoidal velocity profile in joint space. The controller simply follows that pre-planned sequence.

The work divides into two categories:

Category What you build Node infrastructure How the node tracks joint state, registers services, and sends multi-point trajectories Trajectory math The functions that generate the waypoint sequence from the trapezoidal profile

Work through the steps in order. Each one builds on the previous.

docs.title: Steps at a glance
docs.text:
Step Tag What you implement Where in file 1 [BOTH] Add JointState import Top of file 2 [JOINT] _trapezoidal_scalar_profile — 1-D speed profile engine Section B 3 [JOINT] generate_joint_space_trajectory — synchronized multi-joint waypoints Section B 6 [BOTH] Rename node to "trajectory_server" __init__ 7 [BOTH] Replace q_last_ik_ with q_current_ + /joint_states subscriber __init__ 8 [BOTH] Add motion parameters (v_max, a_max, dt_, …) __init__ 9 [BOTH] Rename motion_in_progress_ → busy_ everywhere __init__ + callbacks 10 [JOINT] Register /ee_traj_joint service __init__ 12 [BOTH] _joint_state_cb — map joint names to positions safely Subscriber callback 13 [JOINT] _cb_joint_traj — orchestrate IK → trajectory → send Service callback 15 [BOTH] Replace single-point sender with _send_trajectory(points) Action helpers 16 [BOTH] Rename action callbacks + swap flag Action helpers

Steps marked [BOTH] are also required for the Cartesian service in Part 3 — you only implement them once.

Note on missing step numbers: Steps 4, 5, 11, and 14 are not covered in this document. They belong to the Cartesian planner (/ee_traj_cartesian) and are implemented in Part 3. If you see those markers in your code file, skip them for now.

How to use this document with your code file: Each section references a specific # TODO marker in XYZServerGazebo_TODO.py by its step number. Find the marker, read the context here, then implement it.

docs.title: Part 1 — Node Infrastructure
docs.text: These steps establish the new node structure before touching any trajectory math.

docs.title: Step 1 — Add the JointState import [BOTH]
docs.text: Go to Step 1 in your code.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
XYZServerGazebo.py never needed to know the robot's actual joint positions. It stored q_last_ik_ — the last IK solution — as a starting guess for the next call. This is fragile: if Gazebo is restarted, or someone moves the robot manually, q_last_ik_ no longer reflects reality.

The trajectory server needs the actual current joint configuration at the moment a service call arrives, because the planned trajectory must start from wherever the robot physically is right now. ROS 2 broadcasts this on the /joint_states topic using the JointState message type from sensor_msgs.

Add the import alongside the other message imports at the top of the file.

docs.title: Step 6 — Rename the node [BOTH]
docs.text: Go to Step 6 in your code.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The node name is what appears in ros2 node list and in every log line. Change the string passed to super().__init__(...) from "move_to_xyz_server" to "trajectory_server". Nothing else changes — this is purely a naming step, but keeping names consistent with what a node actually does prevents confusion when debugging a running system.

docs.title: Step 7 — Track the actual joint state [BOTH]
docs.text: Go to Step 7 in your code.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
You need two things: storage for the current joint positions, and a flag that records whether you have received at least one real measurement. The flag is important because a service call could arrive in the first milliseconds of the node's life, before Gazebo has published any joint states. Without the flag, you would plan a trajectory starting from all zeros — which is almost certainly wrong and could cause a violent jump.

Delete self.q_last_ik_ and replace it with:

self.q_current_  = np.zeros(6)   # updated by /joint_states subscriber
self.q_received_ = False          # becomes True after the first message arrives

Then create the ROS 2 subscription. In ROS 2 a subscriber is created inside __init__ with create_subscription. The call takes four arguments in this order: the message type, the topic name (as a string), the callback function, and the queue size. Store the subscriber object as self.joint_state_sub_ so it is not garbage-collected.

docs.title: Step 8 — Add motion parameters [BOTH]
docs.text: Go to Step 8 in your code.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The trajectory functions you will implement in Part 2 (Steps 2 and 3) need to know speed and timing limits. These are kept as node attributes rather than hardcoded inside the math functions, so you can tune them without touching the trajectory logic.

Add these six attributes:

self.v_max_joint_      = np.deg2rad(30.0)   # maximum joint speed      [rad/s]
self.a_max_joint_      = np.deg2rad(60.0)   # maximum joint acceleration [rad/s²]
self.v_max_cart_       = 0.05               # reserved for Part 3       [m/s]
self.a_max_cart_       = 0.10               # reserved for Part 3       [m/s²]
self.dt_               = 0.05               # control step — 20 Hz      [s]
self.lambda_damp_cart_ = 1e-4               # reserved for Part 3

dt_ is the interval between consecutive waypoints. At 20 Hz and a 3-second motion, the controller receives 60 waypoints instead of 1. Finer dt_ means smoother execution but a larger message.

docs.title: Step 9 — Rename the busy flag [BOTH]
docs.text: Go to Step 9 in your code.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Replace every occurrence of self.motion_in_progress_ with self.busy_. The logic is identical — a boolean that prevents two service requests from overlapping. This is a naming-only change, but it must be applied consistently everywhere the flag is read or written: in __init__, in the service callbacks, and in the action response handlers you will update in Step 16.

docs.title: Step 10 — Register the joint trajectory service [JOINT]
docs.text: Go to Step 10 in your code.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
This is the ROS 2 call that advertises /ee_traj_joint on the network. It follows exactly the same pattern as the existing /ee_pose service in the node: create_service takes the service type, the service name as a string, and the callback. Store the result as self.srv_joint_.

The callback (self._cb_joint_traj) does not exist yet — you will implement it in Step 13. The node will still start correctly; the service will simply crash if called before Step 13 is implemented.

You may keep the original /ee_pose service alongside for comparison while testing.

docs.title: Part 2 — Joint State Callback (Step 12) [BOTH]
docs.text: Go to Step 12 in your code. Implement _joint_state_cb(self, msg: JointState).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every time /joint_states publishes, this callback fires and updates self.q_current_. The critical detail is that /joint_states lists joints in an order that is not guaranteed to match your self.joint_names_ order. The controller may list joints alphabetically, while your trajectory code expects them in kinematic chain order. Reading msg.position by index directly would silently place the wrong angle into the wrong joint — a bug that is very hard to spot visually.

The correct approach is to build a dictionary mapping each joint name to its index in the message, then use self.joint_names_ to extract values in the right order.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
def _joint_state_cb(self, msg):

    # Build a lookup table: joint name → its index in msg.position
    # msg.name is a list of strings, msg.position is a parallel list of floats
    # This can be done in one line using enumerate
    name_to_idx = { ... }

    # For each joint we care about, find it in the message by name
    for j, joint_name in enumerate(self.joint_names_):
        if joint_name exists in name_to_idx:
            # Use the lookup to find the right index in msg.position
            self.q_current_[j] = msg.position[ name_to_idx[joint_name] ]

    # Signal that we have received at least one valid measurement
    self.q_received_ = True

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
After implementing, launch Gazebo and the node. Run:

ros2 topic echo /joint_states --once

Check that the joint names in the message match those in self.joint_names_. Then temporarily add self.get_logger().info(str(self.q_current_)) inside the callback to confirm values update as the robot moves. Remove the log line before final testing.

docs.title: Step 15 — Replace the single-point sender with _send_trajectory [BOTH]
docs.text: Go to Step 15 in your code.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The original send_trajectory_goal() receives a flat list of joint angles plus a duration, then manually constructs a single JointTrajectoryPoint. The new _send_trajectory(self, points) receives an already-built list of JointTrajectoryPoint objects and sends them all at once.

This difference is fundamental: sending a full sequence means the controller follows the pre-planned trapezoidal profile exactly, waypoint by waypoint, at the times you specified. Sending a single endpoint means the controller uses its own internal interpolation — which ignores your speed and acceleration design.

docs.title: Key ROS 2 detail — busy_ flag timing
docs.text: Set self.busy_ = True before calling send_goal_async, not after. There is a brief window between the send and any subsequent line where a second service call could arrive and pass the guard check. Setting the flag before the send eliminates that window.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
def _send_trajectory(self, points):

    # Wait up to 3 seconds for the action server to come up
    # If it does not respond, log an error and return False
    if not self.traj_client_.wait_for_server(timeout_sec=3.0):
        ...
        return False

    # Build the goal message
    goal = FollowJointTrajectory.Goal()
    goal.trajectory.joint_names = self.joint_names_
    goal.trajectory.points      = points     # the complete list, not just one point

    # Set the flag BEFORE sending (see explanation above)
    self.busy_ = True

    # Non-blocking send — the callback fires when the controller responds
    future = self.traj_client_.send_goal_async(goal)
    future.add_done_callback(self._goal_response_cb)

    return True

docs.title: Step 16 — Rename the action callbacks [BOTH]
docs.text:
Go to Step 16 in your code.

Rename: - goal_response_callback → _goal_response_cb - result_callback → _result_cb

Replace every self.motion_in_progress_ inside both with self.busy_. The logic is unchanged — _goal_response_cb clears the flag if the goal is rejected, and _result_cb clears it when execution finishes.

docs.title: Part 4 — Trajectory Math [JOINT]
docs.text:
This is the mathematical core of the session. Steps 2 and 3 are defined above the node class in your file.

File navigation: scroll back up to Section B in your Python file — it sits between the kinematics helpers and the node class definition. You will be working there for this entire part, then scrolling back down to the node class for Part 5.

Read the full context for each step before writing any code.

docs.title: Step 2 — 1-D trapezoidal speed profile [JOINT]
docs.text: Go to Step 2 in your code. Implement _trapezoidal_scalar_profile(total_disp, v_max, a_max, dt).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
This function takes a single positive displacement — the displacement of the largest-moving joint in the motion — and returns three arrays describing how that displacement is covered over time:

  • lam — distance traveled so far at each sample
  • lam_dot — instantaneous speed at each sample
  • times — the time axis

It knows nothing about joints, ROS 2, or the robot. It is pure kinematics. Step 3 calls it once and scales all joints from its output.

Assumption: this function always receives total_disp > 0. The zero-displacement edge case is handled one level up in Step 3 (max_disp < 1e-6 guard) before this function is ever called. Do not add a zero-check here — test it with positive values only.

docs.title: Key concept — trapezoidal or triangular?
docs.text:
The first question to answer is whether there is enough distance to reach v_max. A single ramp from 0 to v_max covers:

\[d_{ramp} = \frac{v_{max}^2}{2 \cdot a_{max}}\]

The full motion requires two ramps (up and down), consuming \(2 \cdot d_{ramp}\). Compare this to total_disp:

  • \(total\_disp \geq 2 \cdot d_{ramp}\) → Trapezoidal: the robot reaches v_max and cruises at constant speed.
  • \(total\_disp < 2 \cdot d_{ramp}\) → Triangular: the robot cannot reach v_max. The motion peaks at a lower speed that must be derived from the area constraint.

In the triangular case, the area of the triangular velocity profile must equal total_disp. Since there is no cruise phase (\(t_c = 0\)) and both ramps are symmetric:

\[\frac{1}{2} \cdot (2 t_a) \cdot v_{peak} = total\_disp \implies v_{peak} = \sqrt{a_{max} \cdot total\_disp}\]

This overwrites v_max locally inside the function. The requested maximum speed is simply not achievable given the available distance — the function silently uses the physically correct peak instead.

docs.title: Key concept — phase formulas
docs.text:
Once you have t_a and t_c, sample the profile at \(N+1\) equally spaced instants in \([0, T]\) where \(T = 2 t_a + t_c\). Use np.ceil(T / dt) for \(N\).

For each sample, the position traveled lam[k] and the instantaneous speed lam_dot[k] depend on which phase the sample falls in:

Phase Condition lam[k] lam_dot[k] Acceleration \(t \leq t_a\) \(\dfrac{1}{2} a_{max} \cdot t^2\) \(a_{max} \cdot t\) Cruise \(t_a < t \leq t_a + t_c\) \(d_{ramp} + v_{max}(t - t_a)\) \(v_{max}\) Deceleration \(t > t_a + t_c\) \(d_{ramp} + v_{max} \cdot t_c + v_{max}\Delta t_d - \dfrac{1}{2}a_{max}\Delta t_d^2\) \(v_{max} - a_{max} \cdot \Delta t_d\)

where \(\Delta t_d = t - t_a - t_c\) is the time elapsed since deceleration began.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
def _trapezoidal_scalar_profile(total_disp, v_max, a_max, dt):

    # ── Decision: trapezoidal or triangular? ──────────────────────────
    # How much distance does a single ramp consume?
    d_ramp = ...

    if total_disp is large enough to fit two complete ramps:
        # TRAPEZOIDAL
        # How long is one ramp?
        t_a = ...
        # After removing both ramps, how much distance remains for cruising?
        # How long does it take to cover that distance at v_max?
        t_c = ...

    else:
        # TRIANGULAR — v_max is not reachable for this displacement
        # Overwrite v_max with the actual achievable peak (see formula above)
        v_max = ...
        # Ramp time using the new reduced peak
        t_a   = ...
        # No cruise phase
        t_c   = 0.0

    # ── Build the time axis ───────────────────────────────────────────
    T     = ...                  # total motion duration
    N     = max(1, int(...))     # number of intervals — use np.ceil
    times = np.linspace(0.0, T, N + 1)

    lam     = np.zeros(N + 1)
    lam_dot = np.zeros(N + 1)

    # ── Sample the profile ────────────────────────────────────────────
    for k, t in enumerate(times):

        if t <= t_a:
            # Acceleration phase
            # Velocity is a linearly increasing ramp starting at 0
            # Position is the integral of that ramp
            lam[k]     = ...
            lam_dot[k] = ...

        elif t <= t_a + t_c:
            # Cruise phase
            # Velocity is constant; position picks up from where the ramp ended
            lam[k]     = ...
            lam_dot[k] = ...

        else:
            # Deceleration phase — how far into deceleration are we?
            dt_d = t - t_a - t_c
            # Velocity decreases linearly back to 0
            # Position continues from end of cruise, slowing down
            lam[k]     = ...
            lam_dot[k] = ...

    return lam, lam_dot, times

    total_disp=1.5, v_max=0.5, a_max=1.0, dt=0.05

b) What must lam[-1] equal, and why? (Think about what lam represents physically.)

c) What must lam_dot[0] equal? What must lam_dot[-1] equal?

d) Print lam[-1]. If it does not match your answer to (b), the deceleration phase formula has a mistake.

Now call the function again with total_disp=0.1. Which case does this trigger? What value of v_max does your function actually use internally? Print it to verify.

docs.title: Step 3 — Synchronized joint trajectory [JOINT]
docs.text: Go to Step 3 in your code. Implement generate_joint_space_trajectory(q_start, q_end, v_max, a_max, dt).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
This function takes start and end joint configurations and returns a list of JointTrajectoryPoint objects — the exact format that FollowJointTrajectory expects. It calls _trapezoidal_scalar_profile to get the time law, then applies it to every joint simultaneously.

The key insight is synchronization: all joints must start and finish at exactly the same time. A joint moving 0.1 rad and a joint moving 1.5 rad cannot each use their own independent profile — the slow joint would arrive long before the fast one, producing a curved, uncontrolled path.

The solution is to build the profile only for the leader joint — the one with the largest displacement — and scale every other joint proportionally. If the leader has covered a fraction \(f\) of its total travel at time step \(k\), then every other joint must also have covered exactly the fraction \(f\) of its own total travel.

docs.title: Key concept — proportional scaling
docs.text:
Define:

\[\delta q = q_{end} - q_{start}, \qquad max\_disp = \max(|\delta q|)\]

The scalar profile gives a normalized progress signal: \(lam[k] / max\_disp \in [0, 1]\).

At each sample \(k\), the position and velocity of all joints are:

\[q_k = q_{start} + \delta q \cdot \frac{lam[k]}{max\_disp}\] \[\dot{q}_k = \delta q \cdot \frac{\dot{lam}[k]}{max\_disp}\]

The division by \(max\_disp\) rescales the profile to \([0, 1]\). Multiplying by \(\delta q\) stretches it back to each joint's own range. Joints with small \(\delta q_i\) naturally move slowly; the leader moves at the full profile speed.

docs.title: Key concept — time_from_start in ROS 2
docs.text:
Each JointTrajectoryPoint must tell the controller when to reach that configuration. This is the time_from_start field — a ROS 2 Duration with two separate integer fields: sec and nanosec. It is not a single float.

To convert a float time \(t\) in seconds:

pt.time_from_start.sec    = int(t)
pt.time_from_start.nanosec = int((t - int(t)) * 1e9)

Getting this wrong is one of the most common bugs in this step. If nanosec accidentally exceeds \(10^9\), the duration is invalid and the controller will reject the goal.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
def generate_joint_space_trajectory(q_start, q_end, v_max, a_max, dt):

    delta_q  = q_end - q_start
    max_disp = max(abs(delta_q))   # leader joint displacement

    # Edge case: robot is already at the target
    if max_disp < 1e-6:
        # Return a single hold-point at q_start, velocity zero
        # time_from_start should be dt (not zero — some controllers reject t=0)
        pt = JointTrajectoryPoint()
        pt.positions  = list(q_start)
        pt.velocities = [0.0] * len(q_start)
        pt.time_from_start.sec    = 0
        pt.time_from_start.nanosec = int(dt * 1e9)
        return [pt]

    # Build the 1-D profile for the leader joint
    lam, lam_dot, times = _trapezoidal_scalar_profile(max_disp, v_max, a_max, dt)

    points = []
    for k in range(len(times)):

        # Scale profile to all joints proportionally (see formula above)
        q_k    = ...   # shape: (6,)
        qdot_k = ...   # shape: (6,)

        pt = JointTrajectoryPoint()
        pt.positions  = list(q_k)
        pt.velocities = list(qdot_k)

        # Convert float time to ROS 2 Duration — split seconds and nanoseconds
        t_k = times[k]
        pt.time_from_start.sec    = ...
        pt.time_from_start.nanosec = ...

        points.append(pt)

    return points

docs.title: Part 5 — Service Callback (Step 13) [JOINT]
docs.text: Go to Step 13 in your code. Implement _cb_joint_traj(self, request, response).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
This callback is the entry point for /ee_traj_joint. It orchestrates everything you have built: it checks the robot is ready, reads the current joint state, solves IK for the target, generates the trajectory, and sends it to the controller.

Failures at any stage must be caught and reported via the response object — not silently, and not by crashing. A service callback that raises an unhandled exception will kill the entire node.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
def _cb_joint_traj(self, request, response):

    # ── Guard 1: reject if already moving ────────────────────────────
    if self.busy_:
        response.success = False
        response.message = "Motion already in progress. Wait until it finishes."
        return response

    # ── Guard 2: reject if joint state not yet available ─────────────
    if not self.q_received_:
        response.success = False
        response.message = "Joint states not yet received. Is Gazebo running?"
        return response

    # ── Read the target and take a snapshot of the current state ─────
    p_des   = np.array([request.x, request.y, request.z])
    # Take a copy — do not use self.q_current_ directly below this line
    # (the subscriber can update it at any moment in the background)
    q_start = self.q_current_.copy()

    # ── Solve IK from the current configuration ───────────────────────
    # Use ik_lm — it returns (q_solution, converged_bool)
    q_end, ok = ik_lm(p_des, q_start, self.dh_table_, self.qmin_, self.qmax_)
    if not ok:
        response.success = False
        response.message = "IK did not converge. Check that the target is reachable."
        return response

    # Optional but recommended: log the FK check
    # fk_position(q_end, self.dh_table_) should be close to p_des
    # Log both values so you can inspect the IK accuracy

    # ── Generate the joint-space trajectory ──────────────────────────
    points = generate_joint_space_trajectory(
        q_start, q_end,
        self.v_max_joint_, self.a_max_joint_, self.dt_
    )
    # Log: how many waypoints were generated, what the estimated duration is
    # duration = last point's time_from_start in seconds

    # ── Send to the action server ─────────────────────────────────────
    ok_sent = self._send_trajectory(points)

    # ── Build the response ────────────────────────────────────────────
    response.success = ok_sent
    if ok_sent:
        response.message = ... # include waypoint count and duration
    else:
        response.message = "Failed to send trajectory goal."
    return response

docs.title: Why .copy() matters
docs.text: self.q_current_ is written by _joint_state_cb, which runs whenever /joint_states publishes — potentially every few milliseconds. If you pass self.q_current_ directly into ik_lm, the subscriber could update it mid-computation and the solver would see a changing starting point. Calling .copy() immediately freezes a stable snapshot for the entire planning phase.

source install/setup.bash
ros2 launch myrobot_bringup ros_gazebo.launch.xml

You should see /ee_traj_joint in the output.

docs.title: Call the service

ros2 service call /ee_traj_joint my_robot_interfaces/srv/EEpose \
    "{x: 0.3, y: 0.2, z: 0.5}"

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• Response shows success: True with a message containing waypoint count and duration.
  • Node logs show: IK convergence, FK verification, waypoint count.
  • In Gazebo: the robot moves smoothly, accelerating and decelerating visibly, rather than jumping to the target.
  • Call the old /ee_pose service with the same target and compare the motion. The difference should be clear.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In Part 2 you built /ee_traj_joint: solve IK once to get a target joint configuration, then generate a smooth profile from q_start to q_end entirely in joint space. The Cartesian path the end-effector traces is a side effect — you never explicitly control it.

/ee_traj_cartesian works the other way around. The end-effector is commanded to follow a straight line in Cartesian space at a controlled speed. Joint positions are computed step by step from that line, not from a single IK call at the start.

This is the fundamental difference students are most likely to miss:

/ee_traj_joint /ee_traj_cartesian IK call Once, at the beginning Never What is planned Joint angles over time Cartesian position over time Path in Cartesian space Uncontrolled curve Guaranteed straight line Path in joint space Smooth trapezoid Nonlinear, computed step by step

The trade-off is that controlling the Cartesian path introduces a new risk: singularities. When the robot passes through certain configurations, the math required to maintain a straight line can demand infinitely large joint velocities. You will handle this with a damped pseudoinverse that keeps the motion bounded even near singular configurations.

docs.title: Steps at a glance
docs.text:
Step Tag What you implement Where in file 4 [CARTESIAN] _trapezoidal_speed_value — scalar speed at a single instant Section C 5 [CARTESIAN] generate_cartesian_trajectory — integration loop + Jacobian Section C 11 [CARTESIAN] Register /ee_traj_cartesian service __init__ 14 [CARTESIAN] _cb_cartesian_traj — orchestrate FK → trajectory → send Service callback

Note: All [BOTH] infrastructure steps (subscriber, busy_ flag, _send_trajectory, etc.) are already in place from Part 2. You do not repeat them here.

File navigation: Sections C and D are below Section B in your Python file. Steps 4 and 5 go into Section C, above the node class. Steps 11 and 14 go inside the node class in Section D.

docs.title: Context

This is identical in pattern to Step 10. Add a second service inside __init__ using create_service, this time with name "ee_traj_cartesian" and callback self._cb_cartesian_traj. Store it as self.srv_cart_.

docs.title: Part 2 — Trajectory Math [CARTESIAN]
docs.text: File navigation: scroll up to Section C in your Python file. Both functions below go there.

docs.title: Step 4 — Scalar Cartesian speed at a single instant [CARTESIAN]
docs.text: Go to Step 4 in your code. Implement _trapezoidal_speed_value(t, t_a, t_c, v_max, a_max).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
In Part 2, _trapezoidal_scalar_profile built the entire speed profile at once and returned three arrays. Here the approach is different: the integration loop in Step 5 asks for the speed at one specific instant t during each iteration. This function answers that question.

It takes pre-computed profile parameters (t_a, t_c, v_max, a_max) and a single time value, and returns a single float. The loop calls it once per control step.

docs.title: Key concept — the three phases
docs.text:
The profile parameters t_a and t_c are computed once before the loop starts (you will see this in Step 5). From them you can identify which phase any instant t falls into by checking its position on the time axis:

\[T = 2 t_a + t_c\] Phase Condition Speed Before start \(t < 0\) \(0\) Acceleration \(0 \leq t < t_a\) \(a_{max} \cdot t\) Cruise \(t_a \leq t < t_a + t_c\) \(v_{max}\) Deceleration \(t_a + t_c \leq t < T\) \(v_{max} - a_{max}(t - t_a - t_c)\) After end \(t \geq T\) \(0\)

This is simpler than Step 2 — no arrays, no loops, just a chain of conditions returning a float.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
def _trapezoidal_speed_value(t, t_a, t_c, v_max, a_max):

    # Before motion starts
    if t < 0:
        return 0.0

    # Acceleration phase — speed grows linearly from 0
    elif t < t_a:
        return ...

    # Cruise phase — constant speed
    elif t < t_a + t_c:
        return ...

    # Deceleration phase — speed decreases linearly back to 0
    # How far into the deceleration phase are we?
    elif t < 2 * t_a + t_c:
        return ...

    # After motion ends
    else:
        return 0.0
